articles.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: loose powders have had a glow up
articles.summary: No longer messy and cumbersome, a new generation of powders blurs, sets and mattifies without the faff. I can’t remember the last time I wrote about loose powder because, honestly, there’s been little point.
body: A fine coating of loose powder locks down foundation and concealer like nothing else can – no bridal or TV makeup artist, dancer or performer would be without it. Now, seemingly all at once, a flurry of new generation powders are offering way more for your trouble.

Charlotte Tilbury’s new Airbrush Flawless Blur Loose Powder (£40) is so good that I think she’ll revive the entire category. Its finish is ultra smooth, refined and flattering, and the packaging dispenses with everything that’s annoying about loose powder – no shaking messily from plastic sieves into lids here. The weightless powder sits neatly under a fine gauge mesh and you simply roll over your puff (included) to pick up exactly the right amount, then press on to the skin – even under eyes, where it sets concealer without caking or creasing.
The word “blur” is thrown around like confetti these days, but here it’s exactly right – everything is softer and hazier. It also looks terrifically natural on camera.
points: No longer messy and cumbersome, a new generation of powders blurs, sets and mattifies without the faff.

articles.title: Nicolas Ghesquière takes us into the future for Louis Vuitton show in Paris
articles.summary: Models walk runway at the Louvre with flying cars hovering above as designer envisions city life in a warming world. In silk slip dresses, breezy vented tunics and gossamer layers of chiffon, the models on Louis Vuitton’s catwalk were perfectly dressed for an unseasonably warm October evening in…
body: This summer’s record temperatures were on designer Nicolas Ghesquiière’s mind. “The world is getting warmer, this definitely had a strong influence” he said.

The show was staged in an inner courtyard of the Louvre, the catwalk illuminated by the tail lights of a fleet of 34 flying cars in Vuitton’s signature Damier check raised on stilts above the catwalk.
The contrast between the futuristic set and the historic buildings was an elegant echo of the centrepiece of the Louvre, where IM Pei’s glass pyramid stands amid the French classical architecture.

The future is always on Ghesquière’s mind – his science fiction bent showed up in the models’ beaded silver fringes that were somewhere between space-age hair extensions and sun visors – and this season, he was thinking about life in the cities of the future, his models as pedestrians among flying cars. “I was thinking about a woman walking through traffic, and how in the urban environment we sometimes feel vulnerable and sometimes feel strong.”

articles.title: ‘It’s hard to imagine the fires of July’: a bike ride through the Cairngorms in Scotland
articles.summary: Wildfires raged through the national park this summer, but much of the landscape remains untouched – and autumn is the perfect time to go. In the Cairngorms national park, the bracken is changing from dark green to russet and umber.
body: The wildfire that began near Glenmore and Abernethy on 15 July burned more than 33 sq km (13 sq miles) of moorland and forest. More than 500 firefighters were involved; homes and businesses were evacuated; and the emergency response lasted over a month. Visiting now, it’s hard to see, or even imagine, the damage. Much of the burned area is high on the hill and far from the roads. It’s a huge loss but, in a national park stretching 4,528 sq km (1,748 sq miles), surprisingly easy to miss.

I have come with a gravel bike to retest new bikepacking routes with Kees Wouters and Yannick Ferbeek from Legendary Rides, which offers self-guided tours, and Bikepacking Scotland founder Markus Stitz, who helped develop the routes.

I arrive in Aviemore from Edinburgh on an electric Ember bus, which allows bikes to be booked on board, a welcome development in Scottish public transport. Soon I’m heading out of town through heather and Scots pines, my bike bags stuffed with everything I need for the next few days.

articles.title: A moment that changed me: I was heading for disaster on the Greek version of Strictly. Then instinct kicked in
articles.summary: I was gripped by fear, aching all over – and still recovering from cancer treatment. But Dancing With the Stars was a joyous celebration of survival. It was an invitation I accepted in a moment of madness – and, over the next three months, regretted many times a day.
body: Dancing With the Stars, as it is called in Greece, follows the same format as its UK counterpart, with an identical studio, a matching shiny floor, even many of the same costumes that are hired out and circulated among the 70 or more international versions of the BBC show. Of course, it’s all in Greek – and in the season I took part in, Covid restrictions had been imposed, which intensified its strangeness.

I am British, but by the time of my appearance on Dancing With the Stars I had become a bestselling author in Greece. In 2010, my first novel, The Island, was adapted for a 26-part series, which achieved the country’s highest-ever ratings for a TV drama. In 2020, I was granted honorary citizenship by the Greek prime minister. All of this had made me a minor celebrity.

I never imagined the competition would be easy. The only woman older than me out of the dozen or so contestants was Bessy Argyraki, who had been a Eurovision entrant in 1977, while I was still at school. In the first week, when we found each other weeping in the ladies’, we became best friends. All the other women could do the splits, but we were still struggling to remember basic steps.
points: I was gripped by fear, aching all over – and still recovering from cancer treatment.
But Dancing With the Stars was a joyous celebration of survival.
It was an invitation I accepted in a moment of madness – and, over the next three months, regretted many times a day.
In 2020, I was granted honorary citizenship by the Greek prime minister.

articles.title: Inside Sephora and Vogue Business’s Night Kicking Off a Global Cause
articles.summary: At the Sephora and Vogue Business event during Paris Fashion Week, the beauty retailer launched its global initiative Project Hearts Not Hate.
body: Sephora kicked off Project Hearts Not Hate, its global initiative to tackle appearance-based hate with an evening in partnership with Vogue Business.

The Shangri-La Paris played host to an evening of conversations, cocktails and dinner celebrating the launch. “I wouldn’t call it a project. I think it’s more than a project — it’s really an initiative, a commitment,” Sephora president and global CEO, Guillaume Motte, said in his opening remarks. “It is actually the first time that as Sephora, we choose to champion a cause globally across our 37 markets.”
Left to right: Laure Guilbault, Deborah Yeh, Guillaume Motte, Emily May, Adelaïde Zulfikarpasic.

The executive continued: “People experience hate because of their appearance, and we want to fight back and help change those perceptions. With humility, we hope to achieve this together. While we don’t expect to change the world overnight, every individual can make an impact. As a beauty leader, we want to shape not only our industry, but also how we live and respect one another's differences.”

articles.title: Vogue First! DeMellier's New “Icons” Collection Puts a Spin on Its Bestselling Bags
articles.summary: Five content creators reimagine DeMellier’s hero handbags through their own personal lens—and Vogue Shopping readers get 24 hours exclusive access to shop the collection first.
body: The real test of a handbag isn’t just how it looks with an outfit for a season or two. It’s whether you’re still wearing it years from when you originally got it. Does it withstand daily trips on the train or messy little fingers reaching for it? Does it play as well with your rotation as it did when you first got it? London-based DeMellier has built its business on this notion, the idea that a solid handbag should hold up to real life and outlast every micro-trend that comes pounding on the door.

And for its latest launch, the Icons collection, the brand asked five stylish women, from Montreal-based style figure Grece Ghanem to Paris creator Lena Mahfouf and models Taylor Hill, Romee Strijd, and Rebecca Donaldson, to rework its best-known designs to reflect their own perspective and personal style. “We chose five different women, across generations, backgrounds and experiences, who were already part of our community and connected with our values,” shares founder Mireia Llusia-Lindh. “They are united by a strong sense of self, determination and purpose, and each has forged her own path.”

articles.title: How to Style a Slip Dress for 5 Different Weddings
articles.summary: A bridal stylist shares five ways to wear a slip dress as a wedding guest—whether you're attending a courthouse ceremony or a black-tie soiree.
body: The art of dressing well starts with figuring out which pieces in your wardrobe are true staples and working around them. Too often, special occasions can feel like an excuse to buy a new outfit; weddings are the worst offenders. It’s easy to think you need to pick up a dedicated dress for each different invitation. Trust us, though: The staple you actually need to build a versatile formalwear wardrobe around is one of the simplest—a slip dress.

Look for something neutral, in a mid-to-long silhouette (the most useful for the most number of dress codes)—for this exercise, we’re using a floor-skimming gown in a cool charcoal. Cut on the bias, it skims the body rather than clinging to it, and its quiet shade takes on the character of whatever you pair with it. At a daytime —or more casual—celebration, a single statement accessory can be enough. As the formality climbs, additional pieces, like glittering tennis earrings or a silk pashmina, can up the polish. Think of a slip dress as the wedding guest equivalent of great jeans: an investment you’ll reach for again and again.

articles.summary: The best retinoids, like tretinoin, adapalene, retinol, and retinal, cater to different issues, like acne and sensitivity, so choose wisely. Shop our top picks now.
body: While the advantages of retinoids like retinol —firmer, clearer, and brighter skin—are essentially fact at this point, what constitutes the best retinoid is a bit more debatable. That’s because retinoid is not a single ingredient, but an umbrella term for multiple vitamin A-derived molecules. “Think of retinoids as a family of ingredients that all work by communicating with skin cells and encouraging them to behave in a healthier, more youthful way,” says Azideh Shirazi, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in La Jolla, CA. “The biggest difference is how directly they get to the active form your skin can use.”

articles.title: Would You Pay $350,000 for Argentina's Golden Passport?
articles.summary: Everything travelers need to know about Argentina's new golden passport, including how much it costs and when applications will open.
body: Americans will soon have a new option for dual citizenship in South America, with Argentina on track to launch the continent's fist golden passport by the end of this year.

For the uninitiated, a so-called golden passport is an immigration scheme in which countries give individuals or families citizenship in exchange for large investments towards specific economic sectors. Argentina recently unveiled new investment requirements and application process details for the scheme, which experts say is expected to begin accepting applications by the fourth quarter of 2026.

Argentina’s program is poised to be one of the most popular options on the market, due to the country's comparative proximity to the United States, strong economy, and passport power. The program “provides a notable new option for investors considering citizenship planning, alongside the wider regional, economic, and lifestyle attributes of one of Latin America’s largest economies,” says Dominic Volek, group head of private clients at residence and citizenship planning firm Henley & Partners.
